data.copy:
I sat in the clinic parking lot with a $4,500 quote folded in my shirt pocket.

Two years I had spent on the surgery fence. I'm 56, an engineering manager, and I had googled lower blepharoplasty more times than my fantasy team. The bags were that bad. Steamer trunks.

The consult was fine. The surgeon was nice. The math was not. $4,500 for my lower lids. General anesthesia. Ten to fourteen days of bruises to explain in meetings. And insurance only helps if the skin blocks your field of vision. Mine just made people ask if I got into a fight.

I sat in the truck and could not turn the key. It was not only the money. It was the thought of coming back with someone else's eyes. Surgery is permanent in both directions.

That night I had the deposit page open at 1am, cursor on the button. I closed the laptop instead and gave myself one rule. Before the scalpel, I try the last sane step first.

Not filler. My buddy paid $1,200 for tear trough filler and his puffiness was back inside a week. Not Botox near the eyes, I had heard the droopy lid stories. And not another cream. We all know the creams were a money grab.

The step I found was a dissolving microneedle patch. Here is the honest part. A scalpel removes herniated fat, and some men truly need that. But for a lot of us the daily problem is fluid and deflated, crepey skin. That does not need demolition. It needs drainage and support. 1,500 dissolving micro-tips of hyaluronic acid and peptides, about 0.3mm under the skin, right where the fluid pools. Twenty minutes and the tray goes in the trash.

The deflated look eased the first night. A month in, I look rested in the morning instead of like I went three rounds. The $4,500 is still in my account. Nobody at work knows I did anything. They just stopped asking.

Two guys from my group chat ordered after I sent one photo of the tray.

data.caption: Sale Ends Tonight!
data.copy:
Three months after my husband died, I was invited to dinner only to be told by my best friends I was excluded from our annual couples trip. "We gave your spot to someone else. You have to understand." I smiled. I understand.

For twelve years, my husband Tom and I cruised the Mediterranean every September with the same three couples. It was our thing. We'd plan it together over wine in January, book by March, and spend all summer looking forward to it.

I researched the ports. Found the excursions. Booked the restaurants. Tom handled the logistics at the terminals.

Tom died fourteen months ago. Pancreatic cancer. He was 61.

After the funeral, the calls came constantly. Cassie checking in. Pam dropping off casseroles. Everyone saying "let us know if you need anything."

By month three, the calls slowed down.

By month six, they stopped.

Then I open Instagram on a Tuesday morning. And there they are. All six of them. At a café in Florence. Cassie's holding a glass of wine and grinning. The caption: "The crew does Italy! 🇮🇹✈️"

The crew. Without me.

I called Cassie that afternoon.

"Oh, Susan." That voice. The one that sounds like warmth but lands like a verdict. "We didn't want to upset you. It was sort of last-minute. And honestly, we didn't think you'd be up for it. You know, with everything you've been going through."

She kept going.

"And Italy is a lot of logistics. The trains, the luggage, the cobblestones everywhere. Tom always handled that stuff for you. We just didn't think you could manage it alone."

I sat there and listened.

"It was for your own good, Susan. We didn't want you to be overwhelmed."

Two weeks later, they're all back. Tanned. Full of stories.

And Cassie calls me.

"Susan, I have exciting news. We're doing our annual cruise in September. Mediterranean. And we'd love for you to help plan the itinerary. You always find those incredible hidden restaurants and those excursions nobody else knows about. You're so good at organizing…

⠀
Le tissu est tiré, effiloché, et je sais exactement à quelle heure ça se passe : vers 6 h du matin, et encore vers 21 h.
⠀
Ce qui me rendait folle, ce n'est pas le divan. C'est que le griffoir était à un mètre. Un beau griffoir, payé plein prix, posé exactement là où on m'avait dit de le poser.
⠀
Il passait devant sans même tourner la tête.
⠀
J'ai longtemps cru qu'il me niaisait. J'ai essayé le vaporisateur, le papier collant, la couverture sur l'accoudoir. J'ai racheté un griffoir plus gros. Puis un troisième.
⠀
Trois griffoirs dans le placard. Et le divan qui continuait.
⠀
C'est en lisant sur le comportement des chats d'intérieur que j'ai compris que je me trompais depuis le début. Griffer, ce n'est pas de l'entretien de griffes. Et ce n'est pas de la désobéissance non plus.
⠀
Le geste que fait votre chat quand il plante ses griffes dans le tissu, il le fait pour une raison précise. Et cette raison explique aussi pourquoi une planche posée à plat ne l'intéressera jamais.
⠀
Le jour où je l'ai compris, j'ai arrêté d'acheter des griffoirs au hasard.
⠀
J'ai mis par écrit tout ce que j'ai appris, et ce qui a fini par marcher chez moi :

data.caption: Support Your Kindeys Naturally
data.copy:
I'm a nurse with Stage 3 kidney disease. I tried everything. Here's what actually worked.

I've been a nurse for 38 years, and kidney disease is one of the hardest things I see my people struggle with.

And I do mean MY people. Black Americans are three times more likely to develop kidney failure than white Americans. Three times. I've watched it take aunties, uncles, fathers, church mothers, neighbors. The foamy urine. The burning when you pee. The swollen ankles that never go down. I've had patients tell me they're up 3 or 4 times every night running to the bathroom. Day and night, it never stops.

About three years ago, it happened to me. My own kidneys started declining out of control. I have stage 3 kidney disease. All those years of long shifts, putting everybody else first, not taking care of myself the way I should have finally caught up with me.

Because that's what we do, isn't it? We the ones holding everybody else together. The strong ones. The ones who don't complain. I spent 38 years taking care of other people's health and completely neglected my own.

At first it was just feeling tired after lunch. Then came the swelling. Those sudden waves of exhaustion and brain fog that hit you out of nowhere. By the end of my shift, I could barely think straight. But the worst part? Nighttime. The second I'd finally fall asleep, I'd wake up needing to pee. Again. And again. I'd be dragging myself to the bathroom three, sometimes four times a night, feeling exhausted no matter how much water I drank.

Now I was the one living with it. And let me tell you, every patient was right. It's a living hell.

My doctor looked at my numbers and said, "Well, you're stage 3, but it's not critical yet. Let's just keep monitoring. Drink more water, cut your sodium." That was it. I sat in that parking lot for ten minutes just staring at my steering wheel.

Now let me tell you something us Black folks already know in our bones. The medical system was not built for us. From Tuskeg…

data.copy:
Il faisait 34 degrés. À midi, son chat dormait. À 18h, il était sous perfusion. Entre les deux, aucun signe que sa maîtresse a su lire.
 
« Mais il avait de l'eau, sa gamelle était pleine, je la changeais tous les jours. » C'est la phrase que j'entends à chaque canicule. Et je la crois à chaque fois.
 
Je suis le Dr Marine Faure, vétérinaire en médecine féline. Quatorze ans de cabinet.
 
Il y a une période que je redoute : l'été. Parce qu'à chaque vague de chaleur, ma salle d'attente se remplit des mêmes cas. Des chats déshydratés, des reins qui commencent à lâcher.
 
Une cliente m'a amené Milo, 7 ans. Pendant la canicule, elle l'avait trouvé « tranquille ». Il dormait plus, se cachait dans la salle de bain, mangeait moins. Elle pensait qu'il profitait du soleil. Il ne profitait pas. Son corps rationnait l'eau.
 
Voici ce que personne ne lui avait expliqué. Un chat ne transpire pas comme nous. Il se rafraîchit en haletant et par les coussinets, ce qui est très peu efficace. Quand il fait chaud, il perd de l'eau beaucoup plus vite qu'on ne l'imagine.
 
Et il part avec un handicap : c'est un très mauvais buveur. Son ancêtre vient du désert, son instinct le pousse à se méfier de l'eau qui stagne. Alors il boit peu, par petites gorgées.
 
Additionnez les deux, et vous obtenez une déshydratation silencieuse qui, en pleine chaleur, bascule en quelques jours. Il ne miaule pas pour vous dire qu'il a soif.
 
Et quand les symptômes deviennent visibles, c'est souvent déjà tard. La déshydratation répétée concentre les urines, fatigue les reins, ouvre la voie aux cristaux urinaires (ces dépôts qui peuvent boucher la vessie, une urgence) et à l'insuffisance rénale, qui touche environ un chat âgé sur trois.
 
Le seul vrai levier que vous contrôlez, c'est de lui redonner envie de boire. Et ce qui déclenche cet instinct, c'est une eau qui coule, fraîche, propre. La même eau vive qu'il va chercher au robinet. Ces chats qui harcèl…

data.caption: Read This If You Feel Something's Off 👆
data.copy:
I sat on the bathroom floor at 2am last Tuesday and cried.

Not because anything terrible had happened. Not because someone had died or I'd gotten bad news.

I cried because I was so tired I couldn't stand up properly, and I didn't understand why.

I'm 64. I live just outside Toronto. I've got a husband, two grown kids, a little garden I used to love puttering around in. A normal life by any measure.

But for the last three years, I haven't felt normal. Not even close.

It started slowly. The kind of slow where you don't notice it's happening until you're already drowning.

I'd wake up in the morning and feel like I hadn't slept at all. Heavy. Foggy. Like someone had filled my head with wet cement overnight.

My nose would be completely blocked. I'd spend the first forty minutes of every morning in the bathroom — blowing my nose, clearing my throat, coughing up thick phlegm that tasted like nothing and felt like everything.

My husband would already be up making coffee and I'd still be standing over the sink, hacking.

Every. Single. Morning.

I told myself it was just getting older. That this is what happens when you hit your sixties. Your body slows down. You don't recover the way you used to. You just... deteriorate.

I believed that for a long time.

The tiredness was the worst part. Not sleepy-tired. Bone-tired. The kind where you sit down at 10am and your body just... stops. Like someone's pulled the plug out.

I'd be at Costco — nothing strenuous, just the usual run — and I'd have to lean on the cart because my legs felt like they were filled with sand.

I started avoiding things. Lunch with my friend Diane. Walking the dog past the first block. Even cooking dinner some nights. I'd just stand at the kitchen counter and think, I can't. I physically cannot do this right now.

And I'd feel so ashamed. Because what was wrong with me? I wasn't sick. I didn't have cancer. I didn't have anything you could point to and say "that's why."

I found my best friend unconscious on her kitchen floor with her 4-year-old son sitting next to her, stroking her hair, saying "Mummy wake up."

I need you to read this. All of it.

Because what nearly killed my best friend is probably happening inside YOU right now. And your doctor will never, EVER tell you.

By the end of this, you're going to be furious. Not at me. At the system that let a healthy 36-year-old woman collapse in front of her child — while six doctors told her she was "just stressed."

Rachel and I have been best friends since we were 14.

Shared everything. School. Uni. First heartbreaks. Weddings. She was my maid of honour. I was hers.

She's one of those women who just radiates energy. Always moving. Always laughing. The one organising Friday dinners, planning holidays, texting the group chat at 6 AM about some insane idea she had.

She ran half-marathons for fun. Meal-prepped on Sundays. Drank green smoothies before it was trendy. She was annoyingly healthy. The kind of person who made you feel like you should be trying harder.

That was Rachel.

Until it wasn't.

It started about two and a half years ago.

She mentioned she'd been feeling tired. Not normal tired. Bone-deep tired. The kind where you wake up after nine hours and your body feels like concrete.

I said what everyone says: "You're a mum. You work full time. Of course you're knackered."

She laughed it off. So did I.

But it didn't stop.

Within a few months, she'd cancelled on me three times in a row. Rachel never cancels. This is the woman who showed up to my birthday dinner with food poisoning because she "didn't want to miss it."

Maandagavond 6 oktober is het weer zover en kun je tussen 20.00 en 22.00 uur chatten met slaapcoaches Kim Oversier van Sleepzzz Slaapcoaching en Anouk van de Schoor, slaapoefentherapeut.

Slaapproblemen kunnen in elke leeftijdsfase voorkomen bij kinderen. Van baby’s die veel huilen en weinig slapen tot peuters die niet willen inslapen of doorslapen. Of niet in het eigen bed willen slapen. Of juist heel vroeg wakker worden. En van basisschoolkinderen die ’s avonds niet naar bed willen en eindeloos blijven discussiëren over het tijdstip van naar bed gaan. Tot pubers die moeilijk in slaap kunnen komen. En al wat meer… Alle vragen die op welke manier dan ook te maken hebben met het slapen van je kind, kun je tijdens dit thema chatspreekuur voorleggen!

Ga op maandag 6 oktober tussen 20.00 uur en 22.00 uur naar www.cjg043.nl en klik op de ‘stel-je-vraag-button’ onder in beeld voor een privé-chat. Log in met een (verzonnen) naam en je postcode. Vervolgens kom je in een 1-op-1 chatgesprek met een van onze slaap-experts, waar je gratis en anoniem je vragen kunt voorleggen voor persoonlijk advies! Vanwege het groot aantal chats dat binnenkomt, kan het zijn dat je even in een wachtrij wordt geplaatst. Tip: chat wat later, het is namelijk aan het begin rond 20.00 uur meestal erg druk.

niches.description: Product category / vertical filter (dashboard Meta niches). Use when user asks for a category, niche, vertical, or market — not keyword.
niches.allowed_values: All, or comma-separated codes: CG, AM, GG, JY, GS, HT, BY, BG, SK, WC, MC, SP, KS, TS, HE, PS, DP, HI, FT, OG, OP, TR, AC, AA, BM, FK, SH, SW, EL, FW, WT, EW, FR, GM, PH, EC, WE, SC, BE, MU, PA, CB, CF, CP, DC, CT, HH, SG, YG, CC, PZ, LS, GP, WN, SF, OR, MG, PB. See allowed_niches in response for code→label map. Fashion/clothing = CG.

website.description: Detected store/checkout technology on the landing page (dashboard Website filter).
website.allowed_values: All, or comma-separated codes: SH, TP, BU, LS, CC, SL, TA, GG, FU, CS, LP, FO, SI, GP, XS, YC, HY, DI, MS, SB, PP, WC, TT, TW, PI, GO, SC, FB, MG, WP, SQ, PS, GM, KV, CO, HJ, WX, AR, BC, MC. SH=Shopify, WC=WooCommerce, CS=Clickfunnels. See allowed_technologies in response.

languages.allowed_values: All, or comma-separated: en, nl, de, no, fr, sv, da, it, pt, es, fi, pl, tr, ar, he.

excludeLanguages.allowed_values: Comma-separated: en, nl, de, no, fr, sv, da, it, pt, es, fi, pl, tr, ar, he.

apps.description: Shopify apps detected on the store.
apps.allowed_values: All, or comma-separated app names/ids from dashboard Apps filter. See allowed_apps in response.

excludeApps.description: Exclude stores using these Shopify apps.
excludeApps.allowed_values: Comma-separated app names/ids. See allowed_apps in response.

themes.description: Shopify theme name on the store (exact match).
themes.allowed_values: All, or comma-separated exact theme names from dashboard Themes filter (discover via GET /api/themes).

scaling.allowed_values: rising, stable, declining, nodownscaling, upscaling, downscaling.

mediafilter.allowed_values: videos, images, carousel, dco. Omit/All = all formats.

pagetypefilter.allowed_values: products, collections, funnels, nofunnels. Empty/All = all types.

adscorefilter.description: WinningHunter ad score tier (Established / Has Potential / Unestablished).
adscorefilter.allowed_values: winning (Established), scaling (Has Potential), testing (Unestablished). Requires matching account tier.

lowimpressions.description: Hide ads with very low impressions.
lowimpressions.allowed_values: hide (exclude low-impression rows). Omit = show all.

rankgrowthfilter.description: Within-brand ad rank momentum vs historic rank_history.
rankgrowthfilter.allowed_values: Comma-separated subset of: rising, stable, declining.

minadrank.description: Minimum within-brand ad rank (lower rank number = stronger ad for that brand, e.g. #1).

min.description: Minimum duplicate/active-seen ad count on the page.

minactiveads.description: Minimum active Meta ads on the advertiser Facebook page (total_active_ads_on_page).
minactiveads.notes: find_winning_products auto-applies minactiveads=50 for US when not set (see forced block).

minactiveadsgrowth.description: Minimum page active-ads percent growth over activeadsgrowthperiod.
minactiveadsgrowth.allowed_values: Human percent (25 = 25%); negatives allowed for decline.

activeadsgrowthperiod.description: Lookback window for active-ads growth filter.
activeadsgrowthperiod.allowed_values: 1w, 1m, 3m. Default 1m when min/max growth set. 1w=1 week, 1m=1 month, 3m=3 months.
activeadsgrowthperiod.notes: 14d/2m exist on the dashboard but are omitted from MCP — sparse wlads baselines return empty result sets.

minpagelikes.allowed_values: Integer >= 0. Ads missing the field excluded when min set.

minadspend.description: Minimum EU ad spend total in adspendtimeframe window.
minadspend.allowed_values: Integer >= 0. May require higher account tier; can return upgrade JSON.

maxadspend.description: Maximum EU ad spend in window.
maxadspend.allowed_values: Integer >= 0. 999999 treated as no upper cap server-side.

adspendtimeframe.description: Rolling window ad spend is summed over (NOT a calendar month filter).

minreach.description: Minimum EU reach/views total in reachtimeframe window.
minreach.allowed_values: Integer >= 0. May require higher account tier.

reachtimeframe.description: Rolling window reach is summed over.

mintraffic.allowed_values: Integer >= 0. May require higher account tier.

minproductsonstore.description: Minimum published products on the Shopify store.

minprice.description: Minimum product price on landing page.

mincopylength.description: Minimum ad primary text character length.

minvideolength.description: Minimum video duration in seconds (use with mediafilter=videos).

mindays.description: Minimum days the ad has been running.
mindays.allowed_values: Integer >= 0. May require higher account tier.

from.description: Ad launch date lower bound (Meta started field — when ad began running, NOT scrape date).
from.allowed_values: YYYY-MM-DD. Requires to on same range.

to.notes: To isolate ads running in a calendar month: ad_created_to=last day of month AND fromlastseen=first day of month.

product_from.description: Shopify product creation date lower bound.

pagefrom.description: Facebook page creation date lower bound.

activestatus.description: Legacy dashboard param (no longer applied to ES queries).
activestatus.allowed_values: Ignored — use adstatus or last_seen_from/to instead.

adstatus.description: Dashboard Status filter — recently seen vs stale ads.
adstatus.allowed_values: active (lastSeen or updated_at within last 4 days), inactive (neither field within last 4 days), All/empty (no status filter).
adstatus.notes: find_winning_products forces active. Same as dashboard Status = Active.

sorting.allowed_values: relevance, datefound, mostrecent, lastseen, adspend, longestrunning, reach, adsetamount, consistency, monthlyvisits, monthlytraffic, monthlyrevenue, pageactiveads, toprank, mostsaved. Aliases: rank/top_ad/best_ranked→toprank (asc = best rank first, desc = worst rank first). ad_started→mostrecent. monthly_visits→monthlyvisits. monthly_traffic→monthlytraffic.

page.description: Pagination page index (informational). Deep pagination requires scroll from the previous response — incrementing page alone does not advance the result set.
page.allowed_values: MCP uses 1-based page (1=first page); echoed value is 0-based internal page sent to API.

scroll.description: Opaque pagination cursor. Empty/omit on the first request; pass the response scroll value on the next request with the same filters to fetch more ads. Required to download beyond the first page (especially sort_by=lastseen).
scroll.allowed_values: Opaque string from previous response; empty string or omit for first page. Stop when scroll is null/absent or data is shorter than a full page.

mcp_pagination.hint: Pass scroll_next as scroll on the next call with the same filters to continue. Do not rely on page alone.
